1: COVID-19 and digitalization did change how people live and how sport is performed and consumed, so sport did not escape societal shock. But French and other participation series also show continuity and later recovery or even a slight rise in regular sport after 2018, so lifestyles and sport were not generally “deeply transformed” as a lasting, across-the-board result by 2026-11-15.
2: UNESCO and some governments continued to expand futures-literacy and foresight work after 2018, including World Futures Day 2025 and a Global Anticipatory Policy coalition, which supports a direction of greater currency. Independent public-management research in 2026 still finds strategic foresight largely marginal, so the stated endpoint of far greater currency and impact has not been reached.
3: A 2025 systematic review and other studies still disagree on whether filter bubbles and echo chambers exist, intensified, or usefully describe most users’ media diets. Because the claimed strengthening of both global communication and Filter Bubble limits is empirically contested, the claim cannot be scored on the archived record.
4: Search and generative-AI tools after 2018 made desired information quicker to reach, and work on the “narrow search effect” supports comfort- or confirmation-bounded knowing. But reviews also show information overload and weaker science learning on social media, so it is not established that people “know more overall.”
5: The condition only partly holds. ILGA and other records show expanded legal gender recognition in some jurisdictions, while CIVICUS, ILGA-Europe and reporting on the United States document a sharp 2020s rollback and repression of gender-fluid and trans rights in others. Where the condition holds, civic space is more constrained; it is not a uniform global “stifled present.”
6: Feminist and LGBTQ-inclusive policy work continued in some international and national settings after 2018, so a push toward more inclusive futures is visible. The same window also shows a documented global backlash and rollback of gender justice, so that push does not unambiguously continue as the dominant direction.
7: Democratic backsliding, conservative and ‘green’ backlash, and climate-policy strain after 2018 are well documented and pull toward less equitable climate and civic outcomes. International IDEA and other sources do not show a general economic or ecological collapse, so that half of the claim is not borne out.
